short: France's first tank, and the first to burn its crews in numbers at Berry-au-Bac.
full:
Eugène Brillié at Schneider began with an imported Holt tractor chassis, lengthened and clad in an armoured box with a nose like a ship's ram for cutting wire. Colonel Jean-Baptiste Estienne, who had pressed the case for armoured vehicles on Joffre, got the War Ministry to order 400 in secret on 25 February 1916. The result carried a short 75 mm gun in a sponson on the right side, two Hotchkiss machine guns and a crew of six. The tracks were too short for the hull, so the overhanging nose caught in every wide trench.

Of 132 committed at Berry-au-Bac on 16 April 1917, the first day of the Nivelle offensive, 76 were lost, many burned out when German shellfire found the petrol tanks mounted inside against the hull sides. Later machines were given extra plating and external fuel tanks. About 400 were delivered in all. By 1918 the Schneider was outclassed by the small, cheap Renault FT, and surviving vehicles increasingly did supply work behind the line.
